connections.why: Particle theory underpins how the same particles arrange in solids, liquids and gases
Lighter molecules diffuse faster, linking diffusion rate to relative molecular mass
Electron arrangement decides an element's group and period in the Periodic Table
Isotopes differ only in neutron number, a direct application of atomic structure
Gaining or losing outer electrons to reach full shells creates the ions in ionic bonds
Sharing outer electrons to complete shells produces covalent bonds
Electrolysis relies on the mobile ions held in molten or aqueous ionic compounds
Extended covalent bonding gives giant structures like diamond and graphite their properties
Delocalised electrons explain why metals conduct and are malleable
Balanced formulae and equations are the starting point for mole calculations
Relative atomic and molecular masses convert between mass and moles
Titration calculations use moles and concentration to find unknown amounts
Electrolysis is redox driven by electricity, with oxidation and reduction at the electrodes
Displacement reactions are redox processes that rank metals by reactivity
Temperature changes that affect rate are tied to the energy of colliding particles
A metal's position in the reactivity series sets whether it is reduced by carbon or by electrolysis
Very reactive metals such as aluminium are extracted by electrolysis
Group I trends follow from the Periodic Table arrangement
Group VII reactivity trends are read directly from the Periodic Table
Neutralising acids with bases is the main route to preparing salts
Classifying oxides as acidic or basic builds on acid–base behaviour
Rusting is the oxidation of iron, an everyday redox reaction
Carbon's covalent bonding underpins the homologous series of organic chemistry
Addition polymers form when many alkene monomers join together
Combustion reactions that release pollutants are a key context for reaction chemistry in the environment
Fractional distillation separates petroleum into useful fuel fractions
